::: {.why}
Capacity is not a single number per strategy but a curve, and the ordering of those curves decides what a larger version of your book would even contain.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Rank your strategies by how fast their net performance decays with size, and explain the ordering from turnover and universe liquidity.
- Say what the book would look like at ten and at a hundred times your current size.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Explain the ordering rather than just reporting it: decay speed is driven by turnover and by the liquidity of the names the signal concentrates in, so a fast signal in small caps dies first and a slow signal in large caps last. Check that prediction against your curves and note any strategy that does not fit it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Construct the larger books: re-optimise the combination at ten and a hundred times current size, letting the weights respond to the size-dependent costs. The composition changes, and the way it changes is the most interesting result of the day.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the one-paragraph answer to which strategy dies first and why, which milestone 9 requires.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
The book is re-optimised at ten and a hundred times current size with size-dependent costs, showing how the composition changes as capacity binds rather than only how performance falls.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Which of your strategies dies first as size grows, and why was that predictable from its turnover?
:::
